731.quote_or_event: When Guru Arjan completed the pool at Amritsar and built the Harimandar in its midst, he kept a community kitchen open to all castes and creeds, invited traders from different regions to settle and open their businesses around the temple, and had rest houses built for pilgrims, so that a city grew up with the Harimandar as its focus.
731.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how Guru Arjan deliberately built a living town: a shared kitchen that fed everyone, merchants drawn in to trade, and a community of devotees gathered around the shrine.
731.tie_back: The Kural defines a true country as the place where steady food, worthy people and prospering merchants come together, and Guru Arjan's Amritsar was planned around exactly that combination.
731.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru
731._accuracy_note: A strong practical parallel to the Kural's three constituents of a land, though it describes the founding of one sacred city, not a teaching about countries in general.

732.quote_or_event: “The Creator has given me the nine treasures, wealth and spiritual powers, and I do not lack anything. Eating, spending and enjoying, I have found peace; the gifts of the Creator Lord continually increase. … Millions of obstacles have all been removed, and pain does not even approach me.”
732.explanation: In a chhant celebrating the completion of the Amritsar pool, Guru Arjan describes a place overflowing with God's gifts, where abundance keeps growing and harm cannot come near.
732.tie_back: The Kural's ideal land is rich, untouched by calamity and abundantly fruitful; Guru Arjan's hymn pictures the same unfailing plenty and freedom from trouble, received as divine grace.
732.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 783-784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
732._accuracy_note: Close in imagery of abundance and freedom from harm, but the hymn speaks of the gift of the Name and spiritual contentment (as Sahib Singh's commentary stresses), not the economy of a kingdom, and it lacks the Kural's note that such a land is coveted by others.

733.quote_or_event: Under Guru Amar Das the Guru ka Langar became still more renowned: he expected every visitor to eat in it before seeing him, and Emperor Akbar is said to have eaten there like any other pilgrim. Guru Angad had called Amar Das the home of the homeless and the shelter of the unsheltered, and as Guru he organised twenty-two preaching districts whose leaders transmitted the disciples' offerings to Goindval.
733.explanation: The langar was built to absorb whoever arrived, however many and however suddenly, while the community's offerings still flowed in an orderly way to the centre.
733.tie_back: The Kural praises a land that can carry a sudden influx of people and still pay its ruler's dues in full; Guru Amar Das's langar and offering network did the same for the Sikh community.
733.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Amar Das, Guru
733._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the langar's open hospitality and the offering system mirror the two halves of the Kural, but the setting is a religious community, not a state paying taxes to a king, and the Akbar visit rests on tradition ('is said to').

734.quote_or_event: As Guru Arjan moved from village to village he helped people sink wells and undertake other works of public welfare, especially to relieve the hardship of the famine then gripping the Punjab; a baoli (step-well) he built still stands in Lahore, and at Tarn Taran lepers were treated by the Guru with loving care.
734.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records the fifth Guru's response to famine and disease as practical seva: water works, relief and care for the sick.
734.tie_back: The Kural names crushing hunger and endless disease among the evils a true land must be free of; Guru Arjan's wells, famine relief and leper care were Sikh work against exactly those evils.
734.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru
734._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on famine and disease; the Kural's third evil, destructive enemies, is not covered by this account, and the Kural describes a condition of the land rather than relief work.

735.quote_or_event: “Now, the Merciful Lord has issued His Command. Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
735.explanation: Guru Arjan proclaims the halemi raj, a gentle rule under God's command in which no one harasses or preys on another and everyone lives at ease.
735.tie_back: The Kural's true country is free of quarrelling factions, ruinous internal enemies and gangs that trouble the realm; Guru Arjan's benevolent rule is a land where no one attacks anyone else.
735.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
735._accuracy_note: A strong fit on internal peace; the hymn is primarily about the inner victory over the five passions under God's rule, and it does not single out factions or chieftains as the Kural does.

736.quote_or_event: The Harimandar at Amritsar was demolished by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1762 and its sacred tank filled with debris; when the Sikhs sacked Sirhind in January 1764 they set aside several hundred thousand rupees for its restoration, the foundation of the new sanctum was laid on 19 April 1764, and the temple, bridge, gateway and cleared tank were completed by 1776.
736.explanation: Sikh history remembers the repeated destruction and rebuilding of its central shrine and city; within two years of ruin the community had funded and begun its restoration.
736.tie_back: The Kural says the best land is one that does not lose its richness even when ruin comes; Amritsar, ruined in 1762 and rising again from 1764, is a Sikh example of that resilience.
736.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Des Raj, Bhai (by Sarmukh Singh Amole)
736._accuracy_note: A reasonable historical illustration of recovery after ruin, but it concerns one city and shrine rather than a whole land, and it is an event, not a teaching.

737.quote_or_event: “… wind, water, fire and the nether regions - in the midst of these, He established the earth as a home for Dharma.”
737.explanation: In the thirty-fourth pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes the elements and regions of creation and says that God set the earth among them as a dharamsal, a place where righteous living is practised.
737.tie_back: The Kural lists the waters, hills and defences that form the limbs of a country; Japji Sahib likewise names the natural elements that frame the earth, but sees in them the setting for dharma.
737.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 34), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
737._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both texts list natural features of the land, but Japji Sahib speaks of the cosmos as a field for righteous action and says nothing of hills, rivers or fortresses as the strength of a kingdom.

738.quote_or_event: “Baygumpura, ’the city without sorrow’, is the name of the town. There is no suffering or anxiety there. There are no troubles or taxes on commodities there. There is no fear, blemish or downfall there. … There is lasting peace and safety there, O Siblings of Destiny. … That city is populous and eternally famous. Those who live there are wealthy and contented.”
738.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas, whose hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes Begampura, the ideal city where suffering, fear and inequality are absent and its citizens are prosperous, secure and at peace.
738.tie_back: The Kural names five ornaments of a land, freedom from disease, wealth, harvests, happiness and security; Ravidas's Begampura is adorned with almost the same list: no suffering, wealth, contentment, peace and safety.
738.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 345, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
738._accuracy_note: A near match to the Kural's list of a land's ornaments; the difference is that Begampura is a spiritual city of God's kingdom, and its freedom from taxes stands in tension with the Kural's praise of lands that pay their ruler's dues.

739.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care? From rocks and stones He created living beings; He places their nourishment before them.”
739.explanation: In the So Dar portion of the evening prayer, Guru Arjan tells the anxious mind that God has already set sustenance before every creature, even those born among rocks and stones.
739.tie_back: The Kural honours the land whose wealth comes without being laboriously sought; Guru Arjan teaches that provision is already laid out by the Creator before it is sought.
739.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
739._accuracy_note: Partial: both speak of wealth that comes without straining, but the Kural praises a naturally rich land, while Guru Arjan warns against anxious scheming; Sikh commentators such as Sahib Singh stress that honest effort (kirat) remains a duty.

740.quote_or_event: “The kings had lost their higher consciousness, reveling in pleasure and sensuality. Since Baabar’s rule has been proclaimed, even the princes have no food to eat.”
740.explanation: In the Babarvani hymns, Guru Nanak laments the sack of the Punjab by Babur's armies and lays part of the blame on the rulers, who had squandered their wealth in pleasure and lost their awareness.
740.tie_back: The Kural warns that even a land with every excellence is fruitless without a fitting ruler; Guru Nanak shows a rich realm brought to hunger because its rulers were unfit.
740.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
740._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the ruin that follows unfit rule; Guru Nanak frames the disaster ultimately within God's will (hukam), a dimension the Kural does not share.
